transcript.text: I've run a commercial painting company
for 22 years, doing about $3.4 million a
year. My son just joined, pulled our
numbers, and told me we're leaving 600
grand a year on the table because my
margins are way under everyone else's.
He's probably right, but these are guys
who've been calling me since 2003. Like,
how do I raise prices on people who've
been that loyal?
>> Uh number one is that you're going to
announce that it's changing on new
people as fast as humanly possible. Then
when the people call back to do work,
you're going to say, "Hey, just letting
you know our prices went up. But,
because you've been a loyal customer,
we're going to grandfather your prices
in for the next X period of time." So, 3
months, 6 months, whatever you want. And
then that way, they feel like they're
being rewarded for doing so, but you're
still saying, "Listen, these tariffs are
killing us." Or inflation, or cite
whatever reason you want. The other part
of it is if you're making a gigantic
adjustment that would be more than what
like call it, you know, a 10 or 20%
price rate, which I would encourage you
to go bigger because you haven't changed
them in 22 years, give a reason why that
benefits the customer, which is,
"Listen, we've said that we want to be
the leading person in the space. From a
quality perspective, we no longer feel
like we can deliver the quality that is
going to maintain our reputation at
these prices. And so, out of moral
integrity, we have to charge more so
that we can keep our quality standards
high. This is what we're doing with the
money, X, Y, and Z that's going to
benefit you ultimately so that we can
keep your business not just for the next
year but for the next 20."
